rubric: FROM ASSEMBLER TO C / I/O AND DATA / CHAPTER 8

slides.title: FILE * streams
slides.main: stdin, stdout, stderr are ready at startup; you open the rest.

captions: C has no print statements: output is library functions; a stream is a pointer to a FILE with a buffer and position
Three streams are ready at startup: stdin, stdout, and stderr; you open the others yourself
You own the format, buffer size, and error checks — no Python print or Rust println! does it for you

slides.title: printf
slides.main: Flags, width, precision; returns a character count.

captions: %d and %u — integers, %x — hex, %c — character, %s — string, %f %e %g — floating point, %% — a percent sign
Between % and the letter: flags, width, precision — %08d zero-pads to eight, %.3f keeps three decimals
Returns the number of characters printed, or negative on error

slides.title: Types and formats
slides.main: The format must match the argument type exactly.

captions: %ld — long, %lld — long long, %zu — size_t, %hhd — char: the format must match the argument type exactly
printf takes arguments by variadic rules and knows no types: %d for a long is undefined behavior
For exact-size types, inttypes.h provides format macros; -Wall catches errors if the format is a literal

lines: // prints 0 on one system, garbage on another

slides.title: snprintf
slides.main: Always with a size; returns the needed length.

captions: snprintf(buf, size, fmt, …) writes at most size − 1 characters and always adds a terminating zero; sprintf doesn't know the size — unsafe
Returns the length it would have had with enough room: if the result ≥ size, the text was truncated
First call with NULL and 0 gives the needed length; then allocate and print a second time

slides.title: sscanf
slides.main: Check the field count and set a width.

captions: sscanf stores values through addresses and returns the number of fields parsed — that is what you check
%s without a width reads a word of any length — overflow; set the width: %15s for a 16-byte buffer
In practice, read the whole line (fgets), then parse it with sscanf or strtol

slides.title: fgets
slides.main: The newline stays in the buffer; fgetc returns int.

captions: fgets(buf, size, f) reads up to a newline or size − 1 characters, adds a zero, and returns NULL at end of file
The newline stays in the buffer if it fit: remove it with strcspn(buf, "\n")
No newline in the buffer — the line is longer than the buffer, the rest comes with the next call; fgetc returns int to tell EOF apart

lines: int c = fgetc(f); // int, not char

slides.title: strtol and strtod
slides.main: endptr and errno; atoi reports no errors.

captions: strtol(s, &end, base): end shows where parsing stopped; end == s — no number, *end != 0 — junk in the string
On overflow it returns the extreme value and errno = ERANGE: zero errno before the call
atoi can't report errors: on "abc" it returns 0, indistinguishable from a real zero

slides.title: fopen and fclose
slides.main: Check for NULL; feof only after a failed read.

captions: fopen(name, mode): "r" read, "w" write with truncation, "a" append, "b" — binary; on failure — NULL
Always check the result of fopen; fclose flushes the buffer and releases resources
feof and ferror make sense only after a failed read: while (!feof(f)) processes the last line twice

slides.title: fread and fwrite
slides.main: Don't write whole structs; fseek, ftell, rewind.

captions: fwrite(ptr, size, n, f) and fread: the result is the number of elements actually processed; compare it with the request
Writing a whole struct is risky: padding bytes and platform-dependent sizes; write fields in a fixed format
fseek, ftell, and rewind change the position: write data, go back to the start, read the same data

lines: size_t k = fwrite(a, sizeof a[0], 4, f);

frames.text: padding bytes — junk in the file

slides.title: Buffering
slides.main: fflush and setvbuf; a crash loses the buffer.

captions: File — full buffering (in blocks), terminal — line buffering (at \n), stderr — unbuffered
If the program crashes, the last output without a newline may vanish from the buffer
fflush flushes the buffer by force; setvbuf chooses the mode and size before the first I/O
fmemopen wraps a memory area in a stream: read from a string just like from a file
open_memstream creates a growing buffer: everything written to the stream ends up in a string
tmpfile gives an unnamed temporary file that vanishes on close; all this is the basis of testable programs
stdarg.h: va_list holds a position, va_start sets it, va_arg fetches an argument of a given type, va_end finishes
To pass arguments on, use vprintf/vsnprintf: they take the va_list itself instead of the ellipsis
The format(printf, …) attribute asks the compiler to check the format in the wrapper; never call va_arg more often than arguments were passed

lines: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += va_arg(ap, int);

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Next — byte order, IEEE 754, and bit tricks.

captions: Streams are FILE pointers; the printf and snprintf format must match types exactly, and the buffer must match its size
Read lines with fgets, numbers with strtol and strtod checking the stop and errno; binary data with the platform in mind; remember fflush
Streams in memory make I/O testable; next — data representation: byte order, IEEE 754, and bit tricks
